The system autonomously identified these security flaws without human intervention for initial discovery, then validated each vulnerability to confirm its existence and severity, and finally generated working patches to fix them. Local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities are particularly dangerous because they allow attackers with limited system access to gain root-level control, making this discovery especially impactful for Linux security. The scale of this achievement—948 vulnerabilities—demonstrates that AI-driven security research can now operate at a level that would require enormous human effort to replicate. This work shows how autonomous AI systems can dramatically accelerate the pace of security patching, potentially reducing the window of vulnerability exposure across millions of systems running Linux. The broader implication is that AI-powered vulnerability research could fundamentally change how we approach cybersecurity, shifting from reactive patching to proactive, automated discovery and remediation.

articles.hook: Language models just got way better at remembering what happened.
articles.headline: StateBench reveals how well AI tracks changes across long documents
articles.body: Researchers have introduced StateBench, a new benchmark designed to test how accurately language models can track state changes—like character movements, object locations, or factual updates—across long documents. The benchmark addresses a critical gap in current AI evaluation: while models are tested on reading comprehension and reasoning, there's been little systematic measurement of their ability to maintain accurate mental models of how things change over time. StateBench evaluates models on scenarios where entities or facts evolve throughout a document, requiring the model to correctly update its understanding as new information appears. Early testing shows that even advanced language models struggle with this task, especially as documents get longer or state changes become more complex. This matters because real-world applications—from legal document review to scientific paper analysis to customer support—often require AI to track what's actually true at any given point. The benchmark provides a standardized way to measure this capability and helps identify which models are genuinely reliable for tasks where getting the current state wrong could be costly. The release highlights a blind spot in how AI systems are currently being trained and evaluated.
examples: Feed a document where character locations change five times and check if the model correctly answers 'where is Alice now?'
Test if a model catches when a contract term is modified halfway through versus only reading the final version.
Present a timeline where a fact is stated, contradicted, then clarified—measure if the model tracks the actual current truth.

articles.hook: Meta just made processing 20,000 ML features per request actually fast.
articles.headline: Meta's F3 Lightning cuts ad ranking ML feature costs through merged graph compilation
articles.body: Meta's Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is an infrastructure system for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features that power Meta's ads ranking models. The scale is massive: a single ad ranking request can require more than 20,000 features to be computed and served in real-time. F3 Lightning, an evolution of the system first presented at AI @ Scale 2020, dramatically reduces computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph rather than executing them separately. This consolidation eliminates redundant computation and reduces latency, allowing Meta to serve more complex ranking models at scale without proportionally increasing infrastructure costs. The improvement is significant for any company operating ads systems at Meta's scale—where milliseconds matter for user experience and every percentage point of efficiency improvement compounds across billions of daily requests. The real-world impact: faster ad ranking decisions, lower serving costs per request, and the ability to add more sophisticated features without requiring additional hardware investment. This is internal infrastructure, not a consumer product, but it's the backbone enabling Meta to run personalized ads ranking across Facebook, Instagram, and Messenger.
examples: Compile 20,000+ features into a single optimized graph instead of running them separately
Serve complex ranking decisions in milliseconds by eliminating redundant feature computation

articles.hook: Meta just solved the privacy nightmare every AI company faces.
articles.headline: Meta's PrivacyLib: One Library to Control Privacy Across All Systems
articles.body: Meta has introduced PrivacyLib, a unified privacy control library that sits at the data access boundary within its Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI). Previously, when Meta needed to enforce a new privacy requirement, engineers had to implement the same logic separately across each of the company's diverse data and processing systems — a tedious, error-prone process that created inconsistencies. PrivacyLib replaces this fragmented approach with a single, centralized library that standardizes privacy enforcement across Meta's entire infrastructure. This matters because as data flows through multiple systems — databases, processing pipelines, ML training environments, serving infrastructure — privacy policies need to be consistently applied at every handoff. By consolidating enforcement into one library, Meta reduces implementation burden, minimizes security gaps, and makes it faster to roll out new privacy requirements company-wide. The library effectively becomes the single source of truth for how user data is protected as it moves through Meta's systems. This is particularly important for AI companies handling sensitive user information at scale, where a single misconfiguration or inconsistency can lead to data leaks or regulatory violations. The approach is practical infrastructure engineering that directly supports Meta's ability to ship privacy-respecting AI products faster.
examples: Define a privacy policy once in PrivacyLib, automatically enforce it across databases, analytics pipelines, and training systems.
Add a new data retention rule and have it take effect immediately across all 50+ internal systems without re-engineering.
Audit exactly where user data flows and which privacy controls apply at each step through a single library.
